'''''Pilosella officinarum''''' ([[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]] '''''Hieracium pilosella'''''),<ref name=POWO_77133566-1>{{cite web |title=''Pilosella officinarum'' <small>Vaill.</small> |work=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:77133566-1 |access-date=2019-01-29 }}</ref> known as '''mouse-ear hawkweed''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=HIPI|taxon=Hieracium pilosella|access-date=31 January 2016}}</ref> is a yellow-flowered species of flowering plant in the daisy family Compositae (= [[Asteraceae]]), native to Europe and northern Asia. It produces single, lemon-coloured [[inflorescence]]s. Like most [[hawkweed]] species, it is highly variable and is a member of a species complex of several dozens of subspecies and hundreds of varieties and forms. It is an [[allelopathy|allelopathic]] plant. 

== Description ==
It is a [[trichome|hispid]] (hairy) [[perennial plant]], with a basal rosette of [[leaf|leaves]]. The whole plant, with the exception of the flower parts, is covered in glandular hairs, usually whitish, sometimes reddish on the stem. The rosette leaves are entire, acute to blunt, and range from {{convert|1|-|12|cm}} long and {{convert|0.5|-|2|cm}} broad. Their underside is [[tomentose]] (covered with hair). The flowering stem ([[Scape (botany)|scape]]) is generally between {{convert|5|-|50|cm}} tall, and sprouts from the centre of the basal rosette. The [[flower]]heads are borne singly on the scape and are a pale lemon-yellow colour, with the outermost ligules having a reddish underside. It flowers from May until August and the flowers are visited by various groups of insects, especially flies.<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1111/plb.12328| title = Competition for pollinators and intra-communal spectral dissimilarity of flowers| journal = Plant Biology| pages = 56–62| year = 2015| last1 = Van Der Kooi | first1 = C. J.| last2 = Pen | first2 = I.| last3 = Staal | first3 = M.| last4 = Stavenga | first4 = D. G.| last5 = Elzenga | first5 = J. T. M.| url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/273158762 | pmid = 25754608 | volume = 18| issue = 1| hdl = 11370/caee8d0d-9724-4056-9d45-93162a5a7afc| hdl-access = free}}</ref>

The plant favours dry, sunny areas. It grows well on sandy and similarly less fertile ground types. It produces [[stolon]]s which generate a new rosette at their extremity, each rosette has the possibility of developing into a new [[clonal colony|clone]] forming dense mats in open space. It also propagates by [[seed]]s.

== Ecology ==
It is a known [[allelopathic]] plant, whose roots secrete several substances inhibiting root growth,<ref name="UC">{{cite web|url=http://tncweeds.ucdavis.edu/esadocs/documnts/hierpilo.html |title=Element Stewardship Abstract for ''Hieracium Pilosella'' |author=Carol Piening |publisher=The Global Invasive Species Initiative |date=1988-08-29 |access-date=2006-11-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060918192827/http://tncweeds.ucdavis.edu/esadocs/documnts/hierpilo.html |archive-date=2006-09-18 }}</ref> including its own. It can be controlled through rotation with [[clover]] and grasses where possible.<ref name="UC" />

Recent research claims that ''Pilosella officinarum'' exhibits an [[atavism]] by the reemergence of [[sexual reproduction]].<ref>''Science News'', vol. 171, p. 302</ref>

The plant has been found as an [[invasive species]] in ''[[Sphagnum]]'' peatlands disturbed by peat extraction in southern [[Patagonia]].<ref name=anales>{{Cite journal |title=Efectos de la extracción de turba sobre la composición y estructura de una turbera de Sphagnum explotada y abandonada hace 20 años, Chile |journal=[[Anales del Instituto de la Patagonia]] |url=https://www.scielo.cl/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S0718-686X2012000200003 |last=Domínguez |first=Erwin |issue=2 |volume=40 |pages=37-45 |last2=Bahamonde |first2=Nelson |language=Spanish |trans-title=Effects of peat extraction on the structure and composition of Sphagnum peatland exploited and abandones for 20 years, Chile |last3=Muñoz-Escobar |first3=Christian}}</ref>

== Similar species ==
Shetland mouse-ear hawkweed (''Pilosella flagellaris'' subsp. ''bicapitata'') is similar, but has two flowers per leaf stalk.  It is found in the  [[Shetland Islands]] only, on rocky coastal [[grassland]]. It flowers from May to August.<ref name="The Wild Flower Key">{{cite book|last=Rose|first=Francis|author-link=Francis Rose  |title=The Wild Flower Key|year=2006|publisher=Frederick Warne & Co|isbn=978-0-7232-5175-0|pages=480–481}}</ref>

== Cultivation and uses ==
Mouse-ear hawkweed has become a common introduced [[invasive species]] in North America (where it is found in southern Canada and both north-east and north-west United States), and New Zealand. It is a level C noxious weed in the United States (with higher levels in the states of [[Washington (state)|Washington]] and [[Oregon]]), and a weed in [[Quebec]]. It does not have special designations in other locations in Canada. It is known to be strongly invasive in New Zealand's [[tussock grass|tussock]] fields, where there are no native species of hawkweed, and [[biological control]] measures are being undertaken to control it and other similar species. In Victoria and NSW, Australia, Hawkweed Sp. are declared as State Prohibited Weeds and are controlled under The Bio Security Act 2015. Currently there are several eradication programs operating (often employing volunteers) to locate, prevent the spread of and eradicate any Pilosella (Hieracium) sp. plants.

[[Joseph Pitton de Tournefort]] mentions that blades covered in this plant's juices were believed to cut through stone as easily as through wood.<ref name=laurentienne>[http://www.florelaurentienne.com/flore/Groupes/Spermatophytes/Angiospermes/Dicotyles/103Composees/09_Hieracium/pilosella.htm Hieracium pilosella] in the online Flore Laurentienne</ref>

=== Phytochemistry ===
The mouse-ear hawkweed contains [[umbelliferone]], a compound similar to [[coumarin]].<ref>{{cite journal |first= G. F. |last= Bishop |author2=A. J. Davy |year=1994 |title=''Hieracium pilosella'' L. (''Pilosella officinarum'' F. Schultz & Schultz-Bip.) |journal=[[Journal of Ecology]] |volume=82 |issue=1 |pages=195–210 |doi= 10.2307/2261400 |jstor=2261400}}</ref> The plant produces [[triterpenoid]]s, mainly [[taraxasterol]], but also the 4,4-dimethyl [[phytosterol]]s alpha- and beta-[[amyrin]], [[taraxerol]], and [[fern-7en-3beta-ol]].<ref name="triterpenoids">{{Cite journal|last1=Gawrońska-Grzywacz|first1=Monika|last2=Krzaczek|first2=Tadeusz|date=2007-03-01|title=Identification and determination of triterpenoids in ''Hieracium pilosella'' L.|url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1002/jssc.200600253|journal=Journal of Separation Science|language=en|volume=30|issue=5|pages=746–750|doi=10.1002/jssc.200600253|pmid=17461116|url-access=subscription}}</ref> It has been used in folk medicine,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Willer |first1=Johanna |last2=Zidorn |first2=Christian |last3=Juan-Vicedo |first3=Jorge |date=2021-12-05 |title=Ethnopharmacology, phytochemistry, and bioactivities of Hieracium L. and Pilosella Hill (Cichorieae, Asteraceae) species |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378874121006942 |journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology |language=en |volume=281 |article-number=114465 |doi=10.1016/j.jep.2021.114465 |pmid=34358652 |issn=0378-8741|hdl=20.500.12466/3283 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> and recreationally as a [[Cannabis (drug)|cannabis]] substitute.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Hieracium Sp. - Hawkweed |url=https://eflora.neocities.org/Hieracium%20Sp |access-date=2023-01-16 |website=eflora.neocities.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Berger |date=2019-12-20 |title=Habichtskraut - ein wildwachsender Cannabis-Ersatz |url=https://lucys-magazin.com/habichtskraut-ein-wildwachsender-cannabis-ersatz/ |access-date=2023-01-16 |website=Lucys Rausch |language=de-DE}}</ref>
